articles.title: BREAKING INVESTIGATION: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

articles.title: Canine Country Club in Rochdale Launches New Classes After Passing Licence Inspection
articles.excerpt: Canine Country Club has introduced new puppy sessions and enrichment classes following a successful animal activities licence inspection, enhancing its services for local dog owners.
articles.content_html:
Canine Country Club, located in Rochdale, has announced the launch of new puppy sessions and individual enrichment classes after successfully passing its first animal activities licence inspection. The owner, Stefanie, who recently took over the business, expressed her excitement in a message to customers, stating, "I am thrilled to share that we passed!"

The new puppy programmes will be held on Thursdays from 10am to noon, providing a structured environment for young dogs to learn and socialise. In addition to these sessions, the club will offer one-to-one enrichment classes designed for dogs that may be timid, less social, or older, allowing them to engage in activities in a quieter setting.

Stefanie emphasised that the welfare of the dogs is her top priority, stating, "Providing a welfare-focused program that prioritises the dogs' best interests has always been my top priority." This initiative aims to cater to the diverse needs of dogs in the community, ensuring they receive the attention and care they require.

Local dog owners interested in these new classes can contact Canine Country Club for further information and to book their spots. The introduction of these classes is expected to enhance the services available to pet owners in Rochdale, providing valuable opportunities for socialisation and enrichment for their dogs.

articles.title: Rochdale’s takeaway winning streak continues as Tandoori Flames takes North West title
articles.excerpt: Littleborough’s Tandoori Flames is the latest Rochdale borough business to take a regional ARTA title, following wins for River Beal in Milnrow and Wild Ginger in Littleborough last year.
articles.content_html:
First Milnrow, now Littleborough. The North West Takeaway of the Year award has found its way to Rochdale borough for the second year running.

Tandoori Flames, on Church Street in Littleborough, won the regional title at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), held at the London Hilton on Park Lane on Monday 12 October.

Last year's winner was River Beal Indian Takeaway in Milnrow. And that was not the borough's only success in 2025. Wild Ginger Restaurant in Littleborough also took the North West Restaurant of the Year award.

Three regional awards in two years, all earned by businesses in Littleborough and Milnrow. Not a bad record for the local curry scene.

The 2026 competition attracted more than 1,250 nominations from across the UK. Tandoori Flames and River Beal both appeared on the North West's ten strong takeaway shortlist, alongside businesses from Bolton, Manchester, Wigan and other parts of the region.

Tandoori Flames emerged with the title. The organisers say their judging process considered customer nominations, online reviews, food hygiene ratings and assessments by a panel of judges. That matters because the award is not based on a single enthusiastic recommendation, or merely on how many people happen to vote.

The Littleborough win continues a striking run for neighbouring communities in the borough. River Beal's 2025 title showed that a Milnrow takeaway could compete for regional honours. Wild Ginger's restaurant award in the same year gave Littleborough a victory of its own. Tandoori Flames has now brought another takeaway trophy back to the area.

The ceremony, hosted by presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha, brought together restaurateurs and hospitality professionals from around the country. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh was among the guests.

ARTA founder Mohammed Munim congratulated the winners and finalists and drew attention to the rising costs facing independent restaurants. Food, energy and staffing bills have all placed pressure on hospitality businesses, even where customer demand remains strong.

An award does not tell us everything about a restaurant or takeaway. Prices, consistency, service and personal taste still matter to customers. But these results provide a useful measure of how Rochdale businesses are performing beyond the borough.

And there is something pleasing about where the trophies have ended up. The awards cover a region with far larger centres of population and long established dining destinations. Yet, for two years, the takeaway title has gone to addresses in Milnrow and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily congratulates Tandoori Flames on its 2026 win and recognises the achievements of River Beal and Wild Ginger in 2025.

Have you eaten at any of the three? Tell us what you rate on the menu in the comments. We are always interested in a good local recommendation.

articles.title: Breaking news: Rochdale Daily reaches 86,000 readers in 30 days — thank you, Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily is celebrating 86,000 readers in the last 30 days, thanking the borough for its support and setting an ambitious goal of reaching 200,000 readers by November.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily has reached an incredible milestone: 86,000 readers over the past 30 days. To every person who has opened one of our articles, shared a story, sent us an email or helped us reach a neighbour — thank you.

We are humbled. We are grateful. And, most of all, we are delighted that so many people across our borough have chosen to make Rochdale Daily part of their day.

We built this independent newspaper around a simple belief: Rochdale deserves local news that is open, accessible and free from party-political allegiance. We want to bring you unfiltered reporting — stories that celebrate our communities, champion our businesses, ask difficult questions and hold public institutions to account without telling readers what they should think.

Eighty-six thousand readers in a month means something to us because behind every number is a person: a parent checking what is happening at school, a resident following a council decision, a family looking for something to do, a small business hoping to be noticed or a neighbour who simply wants to understand the place they call home.

We want you to know that we read every email. We value your tips, your corrections, your concerns and your encouragement. Some of the stories that matter most begin when one resident takes the time to get in touch.

And we have a big ambition for what comes next: to reach 200,000 readers by November. It is an ambitious target, not a forecast, but we want more people across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow and the wider borough to know that their local stories have a home here.

If you have enjoyed an article, please leave a comment. If you disagree, tell us why. If something important is happening in your street or community, get in touch. Follow the Rochdale Daily Facebook page and share our articles with friends, family and neighbours.

Your comments, questions and suggestions help shape what we investigate and where we direct our attention. We won't always get everything right, and when we don't, we want to hear about it, correct mistakes and do better.

We do not want this to be a newspaper that talks at Rochdale. We want it to be a newspaper that listens to Rochdale.

To all 86,000 of you: thank you for putting your trust in us. We intend to work to earn it every day.

Please comment, follow, share and stay with us. This is your newspaper. We want to work for you — and for our town.

With heartfelt thanks, the Rochdale Daily team.

articles.title: Queues form from 7.20am as SpudBros Express opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Early customers queued from around 7.20am for the new SpudBros Express outlet on Manchester New Road, with the first 100 customers promised a free loaded jacket potato at its midday launch.
articles.content_html:
Jacket potato fans were reported to be queuing from as early as 7.20am on Tuesday 13 October as SpudBros Express prepared to open its new Rochdale outlet.

The takeaway concession, at Manchester New Road, Rochdale, OL11 3PT, officially launched at midday with a promotion offering a free jacket potato to the first 100 customers through the doors. The reported 7.20am start would put some early arrivals more than four and a half hours ahead of opening.

Rochdale Daily received a report of large queues forming early in the morning. The precise number of people waiting has not been independently verified.

The Preston-founded SpudBros brand has built an enormous following online with videos of generously topped jacket potatoes. Its Express arm is expanding beyond traditional high streets through a partnership with food business Taster and forecourt operator EG On The Move.

The menu includes the Tram Classic, with garlic butter, a three-cheese mix, baked beans, crispy onions and Tram Sauce, alongside the Spudfather with chilli con carne, other loaded options and build-your-own potatoes.

The Rochdale concession is part of a wider plan to bring SpudBros Express to 30 EG On The Move roadside sites over three years. In an opening announcement, SpudBros co-founder Jacob Nelson said the Greater Manchester launch felt particularly special given the business's Preston roots.

According to the launch announcement, the new Rochdale outlet is expected to open seven days a week: 11am to 9pm from Sunday to Thursday and 11am to 10pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Opening-day trading began at noon.

More information about the menu and locations is available at the official SpudBros Express website, www.spudbrosexpress.com.

articles.title: Finalists Announced for Rochdale Business Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The finalists for the Rochdale Business Awards 2026 have been revealed, with the winners set to be announced at a ceremony on 13 November at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
The finalists for the Rochdale Business Awards 2026 have been announced, with winners to be revealed at a ceremony at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, 13 November. This year, there are 34 finalist places across 12 categories, recognising the achievements of local businesses in various sectors.

Categories include Business of the Year for companies with turnover over £5 million and under £1 million, as well as awards for customer service, community engagement, employment, and sustainability. Some businesses have been shortlisted for multiple awards, showcasing the diversity and talent within the local business community.

Notable finalists include Lynne McDermot from The Willows Dementia Hub, Ashley Dixon from Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd, and Danny Simpson from MID Digital Solutions Ltd, among others. The awards aim to celebrate the contributions of businesses to the local economy and community.

The event is expected to attract a wide audience, including local business leaders, stakeholders, and community members, highlighting the importance of supporting and recognising local enterprises.

articles.title: New Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre Opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has reached a significant milestone with the completion of its base build, marking a key development for the Atom Valley Innovation District.
articles.content_html:
A major milestone has been reached in Rochdale with the completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park. This 30,000 sq. ft facility is the first significant development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub dedicated to advanced materials and manufacturing.

The SMMC is expected to play a crucial role in driving the development of the advanced materials and manufacturing cluster in the region, contributing an estimated £107 million to the local economy. The centre aims to foster collaboration among businesses, researchers, investors, and innovation partners, enhancing Greater Manchester's position as a leader in advanced manufacturing.

The completion of the building is the result of extensive partnership efforts involving the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), and The University of Manchester, among others. RDA has spearheaded the physical development of the SMMC, securing investment to prioritise advanced materials and manufacturing in Rochdale and Greater Manchester.

The next phase will involve transitioning from construction to the specialist fit-out of the centre, with plans to bring the facility into operation by 2027. This development is anticipated to create a vibrant environment for innovation and growth in the advanced manufacturing sector.

articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
articles.content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

Source: Breaking Barriers.

articles.title: From historic chapel to bridal sanctuary: Orla Bridal celebrates its launch in Mytholmroyd
articles.excerpt: A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a new chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.
articles.content_html:
A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a fresh chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.

Founded by Littleborough businesswomen Jessica Demain and Delphine Gott, Orla Bridal marked its launch on Saturday 3 October with a celebration attended by family, friends and local businesses who helped bring their vision to life.

The pair have created a warm, welcoming bridal sanctuary, combining the building’s character with sparkling chandeliers, thoughtful interiors and a collection of designer gowns from Justin Alexander, Madi Lane and Modeca. Visits are private and by appointment only, giving each bride the space and personal attention to enjoy finding her dress with her closest guests.

Originally built in 1806, the Methodist chapel was extended to accommodate a Sunday school in 1872. Acquired by The Craggs Country Business Parks in 2018, it was sensitively restored and transformed into offices, preserving its heritage for a new generation.

Now, Orla is bringing something of the building’s original spirit back to its rooms: a place to gather, share meaningful moments and celebrate love.

For Jess and Delphine, that sense of occasion and belonging is at the heart of the business. Their vision is for every bride to feel comfortable, celebrated and free to be herself, surrounded by beautiful dresses in a calm and supportive setting.

Saturday’s launch offered guests a first look at the boutique, with flowers, fizz and cakes marking the culmination of weeks of preparation and support from local makers, tradespeople and businesses.

Orla Bridal is now welcoming appointment bookings at The Chapel, Scout Road, Mytholmroyd.

articles.title: One in seven Rochdale businesses could be overpaying business rates, research claims
articles.excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
articles.content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Videos raise hygiene concerns at one-star Halifax Road halal meat shop
articles.excerpt: Videos circulating on social media have prompted questions about food hygiene at Rajdhani Halal Meats on Halifax Road, which is listed with a one-star food hygiene rating.
articles.content_html:
Videos circulating on social media have prompted fresh questions about food hygiene at Rajdhani Halal Meats, 115 Halifax Road, Rochdale, after footage was shared which appears to show meat being handled outside close to commercial waste bins.

The footage has been discussed on local social-media groups, where residents have called for the circumstances to be investigated. Screenshots accompanying the posts show a person working behind the premises near large bins and commercial equipment. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified when the footage was recorded, exactly what type of meat was being handled, or whether the activity shown breached food-safety regulations.

Separate published food-hygiene information lists Rajdhani Halal Meats with a food hygiene rating of 1 — 'major improvement necessary' — following an inspection recorded on 25 June 2025.

A one-star food hygiene rating does not in itself establish that food currently being sold by a business is unsafe. It records the assessment made by inspectors at the time of the relevant inspection and businesses can make improvements or seek reassessment.

The circulating footage is nevertheless likely to prompt questions about whether further investigation or inspection is required. Food businesses are required to follow hygiene controls designed to protect food from contamination during storage, preparation and handling.

Residents concerned about food hygiene at a premises can report their concerns to the relevant local authority environmental-health service.

Rochdale Daily is inviting Rajdhani Halal Meats to explain the circumstances shown in the footage, including when it was recorded, what activity was taking place and whether any subsequent changes have been made.

The business is also invited to provide evidence of any more recent inspection or updated food-hygiene assessment. Any substantive response will be added prominently to this article.

articles.title: New Whitworth venue Lillie's to serve kindness alongside cocktails with 'Be Kind' initiative
articles.excerpt: Guests at Lillie's in Whitworth will find anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement waiting at their tables as part of a new 'Be Kind' initiative designed to spread a little positivity from one visitor to the next.
articles.content_html:
A new Whitworth hospitality venue is planning to put kindness at the heart of its bottomless brunches by passing anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement from one guest to the next.

Lillie's, which is preparing to open in Whitworth, says its ambition has always been to create more than simply somewhere to enjoy cocktails, food and company. Its owner wants customers to leave feeling a little happier than when they arrived.

That idea has now developed into the venue's new 'Be Kind' initiative.

Every guest attending a Bottomless Brunch will be welcomed with a signature Lillie's cocktail and a sealed Be Kind envelope waiting at the table. Inside will be a handwritten message from a previous guest containing words of kindness, encouragement, positivity or support. The messages will be completely anonymous.

Each envelope will also contain a fresh piece of Lillie's stationery. While waiting for food, guests who want to participate can write their own anonymous message for somebody attending a future brunch. There is no obligation to take part.

The new note will be placed back into the envelope and passed on to another customer at a later brunch, while guests can take the message they received home with them.

The owner originally considered creating a communal 'Be Kind Box' from which anybody feeling low could select an anonymous uplifting message. Concerns that an unrestricted box might not always be used in the positive spirit intended led to the more controlled table-envelope idea instead.

The concept is based on a simple recognition that people rarely know what somebody else may be dealing with behind the scenes and that a small act of kindness, including a few thoughtful words from a stranger, can sometimes make a significant difference to someone's day.

Lillie's says the initiative is its own small way of spreading kindness one message at a time, built around the message: 'In a world where you can be anything, be kind.'

The initiative will launch as part of Lillie's Bottomless Brunch offering when the Whitworth venue opens.

Alcohol is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.

articles.title: Residents raise concerns over anti-social behaviour around Kingsway
articles.excerpt: Residents and businesses are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour around Kingsway, with police identifying retail crime, ASB and road safety as neighbourhood priorities.
articles.content_html:
Residents and businesses around the Kingsway area of Rochdale are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour, saying a minority of offenders are affecting what is otherwise one of the borough's busiest retail and employment destinations.

Kingsway has undergone significant regeneration over the past two decades, transforming into a major business and retail hub with national retailers, industrial estates, distribution centres and hundreds of jobs. Thousands of people visit the area every day to shop, work and access nearby facilities.

However, some residents and businesses say issues including nuisance behaviour, shoplifting, groups congregating outside retail premises, dangerous driving and road safety concerns have become increasingly noticeable in recent years.

Greater Manchester Police has identified retail crime at Kingsway Retail Park, anti-social behaviour and road safety as neighbourhood policing priorities for the area. Officers say they have carried out targeted operations against shoplifting, increased patrols and undertaken road traffic enforcement to tackle motorists committing offences.

Police have confirmed that numerous arrests have been made for shoplifting at Morrisons in recent months, while dedicated traffic operations have also been carried out along Kingsway to improve road safety. Regular police surgeries are also being held at Kingsway Retail Park to allow residents and businesses to discuss local concerns directly with neighbourhood officers.

For businesses operating on Kingsway, anti-social behaviour can have a wider economic impact. Retailers say persistent shoplifting, disorder and nuisance behaviour place additional pressure on staff while affecting customer confidence. Many businesses have invested heavily in CCTV, security staff and crime prevention measures, working alongside Greater Manchester Police to identify prolific offenders.

Residents have also highlighted concerns over speeding, dangerous driving and the use of modified vehicles on Kingsway, particularly during evenings. Although the vast majority of motorists use the road responsibly, police say road safety remains one of their key neighbourhood priorities alongside tackling retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Community safety experts say anti-social behaviour often requires more than enforcement alone. Alongside visible policing, long-term solutions typically involve youth engagement, support for vulnerable individuals, environmental improvements, partnership working with businesses and swift action against repeat offenders.

There have been encouraging signs elsewhere in Rochdale. Greater Manchester Police recently reported significant reductions in anti-social behaviour and wider crime within Rochdale town centre following the introduction of Operation Tetbury, a partnership initiative combining targeted policing with regeneration and community engagement. Officers say anti-social behaviour in the town centre fell by more than 30 per cent during the first year of the operation.

Many residents hope a similarly proactive approach around Kingsway will continue to improve the area, ensuring it remains an attractive destination for shoppers, businesses and investors.

The overwhelming majority of people visiting Kingsway do so without experiencing any problems, and local businesses continue to invest confidently in the area. Nevertheless, residents say continued police visibility, partnership working and prompt action against those responsible for anti-social behaviour will be essential to protecting one of Rochdale's most important commercial centres.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing anti-social behaviour or criminal activity to report it online, by calling 101, or by dialling 999 if there is an immediate risk to life or a crime is in progress.

articles.title: Could Greater Manchester elect its first woman mayor?
articles.excerpt: As the Greater Manchester mayoral count continues, Sian Astley could become the first woman to hold the office if elected, marking a historic milestone for the city-region's devolved government.
articles.content_html:
As Greater Manchester awaits the declaration of its mayoral by-election, one potential milestone has emerged alongside the political contest. If Reform UK candidate Sian Astley is elected, she would become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was established in 2017.

The mayoralty has grown into one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster. The successful candidate will oversee transport through the Bee Network, hold the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, help shape housing and regeneration policy, manage elements of adult education funding and represent Greater Manchester in discussions with central government over future devolution.

Astley entered politics after a career in business and property development before winning election as a councillor in Manchester. Her mayoral campaign has focused on transparency in regional government, neighbourhood policing, public spending and directing investment across all ten Greater Manchester boroughs. She has argued that communities outside Manchester city centre should receive a greater share of future funding and infrastructure projects.

If elected, Astley would follow Tony Lloyd and Andy Burnham, both of whom held the office before her. While women have led councils and held senior public roles across Greater Manchester, the directly elected mayoralty has so far only been occupied by men.

The possibility of the city-region electing its first female mayor has attracted attention beyond party politics. Supporters describe it as an opportunity to broaden representation in one of England's most significant devolved offices, while political opponents have continued to debate her policies rather than the historical significance of her candidacy.

The election itself follows Andy Burnham's departure after almost a decade in office. During that time, the role expanded considerably through devolution agreements, making the mayor responsible for decisions that affect millions of residents across Rochdale, Manchester, Salford, Bolton, Bury, Oldham, Stockport, Tameside, Trafford and Wigan.

Whatever the outcome, the by-election represents a significant moment for Greater Manchester. Voters are choosing not only who will lead the combined authority but also who will inherit responsibility for some of the region's most important public services. If the result confirms Astley's election, it would also mark the first time a woman has held the office, adding a new chapter to the history of Greater Manchester's devolved government.

The official declaration is expected once counting has concluded. Until then, the result remains subject to the completion of the count and formal confirmation by the returning officer.

articles.title: Who is Sian Astley? The businesswoman hoping to reshape Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Businesswoman, councillor and Reform UK's Greater Manchester mayoral candidate, Sian Astley has rapidly become one of the region's most talked-about political figures. Here's a closer look at her background, campaign and policies.
articles.content_html:
Until recently, Sian Astley was better known for property development and television appearances than frontline politics. Today, the Reform UK councillor is one of the party's most recognisable figures in Greater Manchester, having been selected to contest the mayoral by-election following Andy Burnham's departure from the role.

Astley's political rise has been rapid. Earlier this year she won the Baguley ward on Manchester City Council, ending more than half a century of Labour representation in the area. She now leads Reform UK's group on the council, giving the party a significantly higher profile in one of Labour's traditional strongholds.

Away from politics, Astley runs a design and property business and has appeared on national television discussing housing, renovation and landlord issues. A graduate of the University of Manchester, she has frequently argued that politics benefits from representatives with experience outside Westminster and local government. Speaking after her selection, she said she wanted 'real people with real life experience' making decisions that affect local communities.

Her campaign centred on a message that Greater Manchester has become too heavily dominated by a single political party. Astley argued that decades of Labour control across many parts of the city-region had reduced scrutiny and accountability, claiming residents deserved greater transparency over how public money is spent. Reform UK's campaign presented itself as offering robust opposition rather than continuity.

One of Astley's headline pledges was to review major contracts and spending decisions taken during Andy Burnham's time as mayor. She proposed examining combined authority spending on development projects, reviewing expenditure connected to the abandoned Clean Air Zone proposals and increasing public access to information about regional decision-making. Reform UK argued that taxpayers should have greater visibility over how devolved budgets are allocated.

Crime and community safety formed another central pillar of her campaign. Reform UK proposed increasing police visibility, taking a tougher approach to knife crime, expanding the use of stop-and-search powers, tackling shoplifting and antisocial behaviour, and prioritising neighbourhood policing. The party argued that public confidence in policing had declined and that stronger enforcement was needed to improve safety across Greater Manchester.

Transport policy also featured prominently. Astley criticised spending on what she described as underused cycling infrastructure and opposed introducing additional charges on motorists. She argued that investment should be distributed more evenly across Greater Manchester rather than concentrating predominantly on Manchester city centre, saying outer boroughs such as Rochdale, Bolton and Wigan deserved a larger share of future transport and regeneration funding.

Economic development was another recurring theme. Reform UK's manifesto called for greater support for high streets, road maintenance and local businesses, alongside efforts to reduce what the party described as unnecessary expenditure within the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Astley argued that improving everyday infrastructure would deliver more visible benefits to residents than prestige projects concentrated in the regional centre.

Immigration also featured in Reform UK's regional campaign, although many aspects remain matters for national government rather than the Mayor of Greater Manchester. The party proposed greater transparency around asylum accommodation, opposition to the use of hotels for asylum seekers and stronger cooperation with councils on community impacts. Supporters argued these proposals reflected public concerns, while critics questioned how much influence a metro mayor could realistically exercise over national immigration policy.

Like every candidate in the contest, Astley also faced criticism during the campaign. Political opponents challenged the practicality of some of Reform UK's proposals, particularly where powers rest with Westminster rather than the combined authority. There was also discussion after Astley withdrew from one mayoral hustings organised by The Mill, with Astley stating she objected to the exclusion of independent candidate Marcus Farmer, while organisers maintained their own position on participation.

Whatever the election result, few would dispute that Astley has helped establish Reform UK as a more visible force in Greater Manchester politics. Her victory in Baguley demonstrated the party's ability to make gains in areas long considered Labour strongholds, and her mayoral campaign brought Reform's message before voters across all ten boroughs.

The longer-term question is whether that momentum can be sustained. Metro mayoral elections often provide smaller parties with greater exposure than they receive during local elections, but converting visibility into long-term electoral success is a more difficult task. Reform UK will likely judge Astley's campaign not solely by the final vote share but by whether it has expanded the party's organisation, profile and support across Greater Manchester.

As Greater Manchester enters a post-Burnham political era, Astley's campaign reflects wider changes taking place in British politics. Voters are increasingly presented with alternatives beyond the traditional two-party contest, while regional elections are becoming an important testing ground for emerging political movements. Whether Reform UK can translate growing national support into sustained regional influence remains to be seen, but Sian Astley's campaign has undoubtedly ensured the party is now part of that conversation.
